results.note: Marzuk printed p.1796 explicitly selects hyperthermia cases from 1990 through 1995, identifies 10 with benzoylecgonine, and gives median daily maximum 30.9°C and range 17.2–39.4°C. The index sample is 1382 cocaine-overdose deaths over 1096 days in 1990–1992. Printed pp.1796–1797 say the threshold was based on both the hyperthermia-date median and index plot, and subsequent analyses used 1993–1995. Thus the proposed qualification about the heat-death sampling window overlapping the test years is a supported inference; it does not claim a demonstrated amount of bias. PDF pp.2–3 and the locator are correct.

Crandall printed p.788 reports the greater progressive esophageal-temperature increase with cocaine, P<0.001; p.787 specifies repeated-measures analysis for responses throughout heat stress. The text provides no numerical final temperature contrast. My independently tick-calibrated 300dpi Figure 1 bottom-panel reading is approximately 37.79°C versus 37.55°C, difference about 0.24°C, at approximately 38 minutes. The figure legend states mean ±SE and P<0.001 for cocaine versus lidocaine. This supports the proposed approximate plot reading, with its raw-data and risk-threshold limitations. PDF p.4 and the locator are correct.

Definition, normalization, text values, missing number contributing at 37.86°C, conductance plot reading, and Figure 1 mean-curve observation are supported. My own 300dpi Figure 2 sweat-axis calibration puts the final dotted lidocaine curve near 1.05 mg/cm²/min, rather than 1.07. Also the Figure 2 legend does identify the treatment contrast (cocaine versus lidocaine); what it leaves unspecified is the temperature/endpoint or exact statistical term behind P<.01. Statistical Analysis describes repeated-measures comparisons throughout heat stress, so the different P labels alone are not a proven error in a common endpoint test. A complete corrected extraction and expanded locator are supplied.
results.corrected_extracted: Cutaneous vascular conductance is the laser-Doppler forearm blood-flow signal divided by mean arterial pressure, normalized to the maximum at that site; it is not flow alone. Site maximum was assessed after local skin heating to 42°C for 30 minutes. Results text at the stated highest common oesophageal temperature, 37.86°C, gives conductance 49±9 versus 70±5% of maximum (P=.03), and sweat rate 0.8±0.2 versus 1.0±0.1 mg/cm²/min (P=.04), for cocaine versus lidocaine. Seven people were enrolled, but the number contributing to this highest-temperature comparison is not stated. Independent approximate readings of the final curves on a 300dpi Figure 2 are about 54–55 versus 67% of maximum and about 0.86 versus 1.05 mg/cm²/min; these plotted endpoints differ numerically from the text values. The Figure 2 legend states mean±SE and P<.01 for cocaine versus lidocaine. Statistical Analysis describes two-way repeated-measures analysis of responses throughout heat stress, but the legend does not specify whether its P label denotes that full-response comparison or a particular temperature/endpoint comparison. The different significance labels therefore do not prove inconsistent results for the same endpoint test. The reported information does not resolve the numerical text/plot discrepancy, and no reconciled analysis is substituted. Figure 1’s mean lidocaine curve also ends below 37.86°C.
